original_question: Consider a Hamiltonian system whose linearized operator, for example -Delta_f + v, has continuous spectrum containing an interval. Can such a system admit any KAM tori, even in the case where the Hamiltonian itself may still have short-range interactions?
target_in_paper: Section 2, Problem 2.9: whether a short-range infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian system can have any KAM tori when its linearized operator (for example, -Delta_f + v) has continuous spectrum consisting of an interval.
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper’s actual open problem. It correctly identifies the example linearized operator -Delta_f + v, the key spectral feature that the continuous spectrum includes an interval, and the central question of whether any KAM tori can still exist even when the system/nonlinearity is short range.
missing_details: The problem belongs to Section 2, so the intended setting is the study of finite-dimensional KAM tori for infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian systems, motivated by quasi-periodic breathers on lattices, not the Section 1 problem about infinite-dimensional tori with slowly decaying actions.

The surrounding examples are lattice Hamiltonians such as the discrete nonlinear wave equation q¨_j = ((-Delta_f + v)q)_j - dU/dq_j(q), j in Z^d, and the discrete nonlinear Schrodinger equation stated in Theorem 2.6.

In the nearby context, 'short range' refers to the nonlinear/coupling part of the Hamiltonian, as encoded by the local/nearest-neighbor hypotheses (2.2)-(2.4), or more generally by the exponentially decaying interaction condition (2.14), not to the spectral type of the linearized operator.

The sharp contrast used by the paper is with the pure-point case: Theorem 2.6 says that when Omega^2 = -Delta_f + v has pure point spectrum, even dense in an interval, there are rich quasi-periodic breathers for the short-range discrete wave and discrete NLS systems.

The motivating continuous-spectrum example appears in Remark 2.7: for the coupled lattice equation (2.6), if W(x) = (1/2)x^2 + ..., then the linearized system has continuous spectrum equal to the whole interval [beta, beta + 1].

The paper’s formulation is purely existential and qualitative: it asks whether there are any KAM tori at all under this spectral scenario, and then adds the heuristic comment that 'in general, the answer tends to be no.'
refined_question: In the Section 2 setting of short-range infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian systems, suppose the linearized operator of the system—e.g. Omega^2 = -Delta_f + v in the discrete nonlinear wave/discrete nonlinear Schrodinger examples—has continuous spectrum consisting of an interval (for instance, the interval [beta, beta + 1] arising from the linearization of the coupled lattice equation (2.6) when W(x) = (1/2)x^2 + ...). Can such a system nevertheless admit any KAM tori?
justification: The draft is essentially a paraphrase of Section 2, Problem 2.9. The nearby context first gives positive KAM results for the opposite spectral regime: Theorem 2.6 states that if Omega^2 = -Delta_f + v has pure point spectrum, possibly dense in an interval, then there are rich quasi-periodic breathers for the discrete nonlinear wave and discrete nonlinear Schrodinger equations. Remark 2.7 then explains why this spectral distinction matters, noting that in the model (2.6), taking W(x) = (1/2)x^2 + ... produces continuous spectrum equal to [beta, beta + 1], and this leads directly to Problem 2.9. The short-range hypothesis relevant here is the Section 2 notion encoded in (A2), (2.2)-(2.4), and the exponential-decay variant (2.14).
